L00001: # SQL Generation Evaluation
L00002: 
L00003: This repository contains the code that Defog uses for the evaluation of generated SQL. It's based off the schema from the [Spider](https://github.com/taoyds/spider), but with a new set of hand-selected questions and queries grouped by query category. For an in-depth look into our process of creating this evaluation approach, see [this](https://defog.ai/blog/open-sourcing-sqleval/).
L00004: 
L00005: ## Introduction
L00006: 
L00007: Our testing procedure comprises the following steps. For each question/query pair:
L00008: 
L00009: 1. We generate a SQL query (possibly from an LLM).
L00010: 2. We run both the "gold" query and the generated query on their respective database to obtain 2 dataframes with the results.
L00011: 3. We compare the 2 dataframes using an "exact" and a "subset" match. TODO add link to blogpost.
L00012: 4. We log these alongside other metrics of interest (e.g. tokens used, latency) and aggregate the results for reporting.
L00013: 
L00014: ## Getting Started
L00015: 
L00016: This is a comprehensive set of instructions that assumes basic familiarity with the command line, Docker, running SQL queries on a database, and common Python data manipulation libraries (e.g. pandas).
L00017: 
L00018: ### Install Dependencies
L00019: 
L00020: Firstly, clone the repository where we store our database data and schema. Install all Python libraries listed in the `requirements.txt` file. You would also need to download a spacy model if you're using the NER heuristic for our [metadata-pruning method](https://github.com/defog-ai/sql-eval/blob/main/utils/pruning.py) (set by any values of the `c` parameter that is  more than 0, more below). Finally, install the library.
L00021: 
L00022: ```bash
L00023: git clone https://github.com/defog-ai/defog-data.git
L00024: cd defog-data
L00025: pip install -r requirements.txt
L00026: pip install -e .
L00027: ```
L00028: 
L00029: ### Start Postgres Instance
L00030: 
L00031: Next, you would need to set up the databases that the queries are executed on. We use Postgres here, since it is the most common OSS database with the widest distribution and usage in production. In addition, we would recommend using Docker to do this, as it is the easiest way to get started. You can install Docker [here](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/).
L00032: 
L00033: Once you have Docker installed, you can create the Docker container and start the Postgres database using the following commands. We recommend mounting a volume on `data/postgres` to persist the data, as well as `data/export` to make it easier to import the data. To create the container, run:
L00034: 
L00035: ```bash
L00036: mkdir data/postgres data/export
L00037: docker create --name postgres-sql-eval -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres -p 5432:5432 -v $(pwd)/data/postgres:/var/lib/postgresql/data -v $(pwd)/data/export:/export postgres:16-alpine
L00038: ```
L00039: 
L00040: To start the container, run:
L00041: 
L00042: ```bash
L00043: docker start postgres-sql-eval
L00044: ```
L00045: 
L00046: If you want to reset the Postgres server instance's state (e.g. memory leaks from transient connections), you can turn it off (and start it back up after):
L00047: 
L00048: ```bash
L00049: docker stop postgres-sql-eval
L00050: # see that the container is still there:
L00051: docker container list -a
L00052: ```
L00053: 
L00054: Some notes:
L00055: 
L00056: - You would need to stop other Postgres instances listening on port 5432 before running the above command.
L00057: - You only need to run the `docker create ...` once to create the image, and then subsequently only `docker start/stop postgres-sql-eval`.
L00058: - The data is persisted in `data/postgres`, so turning it off isn't critical. On the other hand, if you delete the `data/postgres` folder, then all is lost T.T
L00059: - While we will use Docker for deploying Postgres and the initialization, you are free to modify the scripts/instructions to work with your local installation.
L00060: 
L00061: ### Import Data into Postgres
L00062: 
L00063: The data for importing is in the `defog-data` repository which we cloned earlier. Each folder contains the metadata and data corresponding to a single database (e.g. `academic` contains all the data required to reload the 'academic' database). We assume that you have a `psql` client installed locally. We will create a new database in our postgres instance for each of the 7 SQL databases with the following commands:
L00064: 
L00065: ```bash
L00066: # set the following environment variables
L00067: cd defog-data # if you're not already in the defog-data directory
L00068: export DBPASSWORD="postgres"
L00069: export DBUSER="postgres"
L00070: export DBHOST="localhost"
L00071: export DBPORT=5432
L00072: ./setup.sh
L00073: ```
L00074: 
L00075: ### Import Data into Snowflake
L00076: 
L00077: Should you wish to import the data into Snowflake, the setup instructions are also in the `defog-data` repository. After installing the [Snowflake CLI](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowsql-install-config), configure your credentials as per the [docs](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowsql-config) and set them as environment variables like below, then run the setup command.
L00078: 
L00079: ```sh
L00080: export SFDBPASSWORD="your_password"
L00081: export SFDBUSER="your_username"
L00082: export SFDBACCOUNT="your_account"
L00083: export SFDBWAREHOUSE="your_warehouse"
L00084: ./setup_snowflake.sh
L00085: ```
L00086: 
L00087: Note that during evaluation you'll have to use the `_snowflake` question files in `/data`. The queries been modified to be valid on Snowflake databases.
L00088: 
L00089: ### Import Data into BigQuery, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server
L00090: 
L00091: The setup instructions for these database management systems are found in the `defog-data` repository. Configure your credentials accordingly, set up your environment variables, then translate and import the eval databases with the command:
L00092: 
L00093: ```python
L00094: python translate_ddl_dialect.py
L00095: ```
L00096: 
L00097: During evaluation, you'll have to set the right `--db_type` flag and use the corresponding `_{dialect}` question files in `/data`.
L00098: 
L00099: ### Using Private Data (Optional)
L00100: 
L00101: If you have a private dataset that you do not want to make publicly available but would still like to repurpose the code here for evaluations, you can do so by following the steps below.
L00102: 
L00103: - Begin by creating a separate git repository for your private data, that has a `setup.py` file, similar to [defog-data](https://github.com/defog-ai/defog-data).
L00104: - Create the metadata and data files, and import them into your database. This is to allow our evaluation framework to run the generated queries with some actual data. You can refer to `defog-data`'s [metadata objects](https://github.com/defog-ai/defog-data/blob/main/defog_data/metadata.py) for the schema, and [setup.sh](https://github.com/defog-ai/defog-data/blob/main/setup.sh) as an example on how import the data into your database. We do not prescribe any specific folder structure, and leave it to you to decide how you want to organize your data, so long as you can import it into your database easily.
L00105: - To use our metadata pruning utilities, you would need to have the following defined:
L00106:   - A way to define joinable columns between tables. In our case, we call a dictionary [columns_join](https://github.com/defog-ai/defog-data/blob/db8c3d4c4004144d2b3ff5a2701529f5545f520f/defog_data/supplementary.py#L233) of database name to a nested dictionary of table tuples to column name tuples. You can refer to the raw data for an example of how we generate this dictionary.
L00107: 
L00108: Once all of the 3 above steps have completed, you would need to
L00109: 
L00110: - Install your data library as a dependency, by running `pip install -e .` (-e to automatically incorporate edits without reinstalling)
L00111: - Replace the associated function calls and variables in [prune_metadata_str](utils/pruning.py#L165) with your own imported functions and variables. Note that you might not name your package/module `defog_data_private.supplementary`, so do modify accordingly.
L00112: 
L00113: Some things to take note of:
L00114: 
L00115: - If you do not populate your database with data (ie only create the tables without inserting data), you would return empty dataframes most of the time (regardless of whether the query generated was what you want), and it would result in results matching all the time and generate a lot of false positives. Hence, you might want to consider populating your database with some meaningful data that would return different results if the queries should be different from what you want.
L00116: - If testing out on your private data, you would also need to change the questions file to point to your own questions file (tailored to your database schema).
L00117: 
L00118: ### Runner
L00119: 
L00120: The runner calls is responsible for handling the configuration of work (e.g. parallelization / batching / model selected etc.) for each question/query pair.
L00121: 
L00122: We have provided a few common runners: `runners/openai_runner.py` for calling OpenAI's API (with parallelization support), `runners/anthropic_runner` for calling Anthropic's API, `runners/hf_runner.py` for calling a local Hugging Face model and finally, `runners/api_runner.py` makes it possible to use a custom API for evaluation.
L00123: 
L00124: ## Running the Test
L00125: 
L00126: ### OpenAI
L00127: 
L00128: Remember to have your API key (`OPENAI_API_KEY` or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) set as an environment variable before running the test if you plan to call the OpenAI or Anthropic/other LLM API's accordingly.
L00129: 
L00130: To test it out with just 10 questions (instead of all 200), parallelized across 5 :
L00131: 
L00132: ```bash
L00133: python main.py \
L00134:   -db postgres \
L00135:   -q "data/questions_gen_postgres.csv" "data/instruct_basic_postgres.csv" "data/instruct_advanced_postgres.csv" \
L00136:   -o results/openai_classic.csv results/openai_basic.csv results/openai_advanced.csv \
L00137:   -g oa \
L00138:   -f prompts/prompt_openai.json \
L00139:   -m o3-mini \
L00140:   -p 5 \
L00141:   -c 0
L00142: ```
L00143: 
L00144: If testing with the latest `o1-*` models (which do not support system prompts), you should use a different prompt file, reduce parallel requests and increase the timeout:
L00145: ```bash
L00146: python main.py \
L00147:   -db postgres \
L00148:   -q "data/questions_gen_postgres.csv" "data/instruct_basic_postgres.csv" "data/instruct_advanced_postgres.csv" \
L00149:   -o results/openai_o1mini_classic.csv results/openai_o1mini_basic.csv results/openai_o1mini_advanced.csv \
L00150:   -g oa \
L00151:   -f prompts/prompt_openai_o1.json \
L00152:   -m o1-mini \
L00153:   -p 1 \
L00154:   -t 120 \
L00155:   -c 0
L00156: ```
L00157: 
L00158: ### Anthropic
L00159: 
L00160: To test out the full suite of questions for claude-3:
L00161: 
L00162: ```bash
L00163: python main.py \
L00164:   -db postgres \
L00165:   -q "data/questions_gen_postgres.csv" "data/instruct_basic_postgres.csv" "data/instruct_advanced_postgres.csv" \
L00166:   -o results/claude3_classic.csv results/claude3_basic.csv results/claude3_advanced.csv \
L00167:   -g anthropic \
L00168:   -f prompts/prompt_anthropic.md \
L00169:   -m claude-3-opus-20240229 \
L00170:   -p 5 \
L00171:   -c 0
L00172: ```
L00173: 
L00174: ### Hugging Face
L00175: 
L00176: To test it out with our fine-tuned sql model with just 10 questions (instead of all 200):
L00177: 
L00178: ```bash
L00179: # use the -W option to ignore warnings about sequential use of transformers pipeline
L00180: python -W ignore main.py \
L00181:   -db postgres \
L00182:   -q "data/questions_gen_postgres.csv" "data/instruct_basic_postgres.csv" "data/instruct_advanced_postgres.csv" \
L00183:   -o results/hf_classic.csv results/hf_basic.csv results/hf_advanced.csv \
L00184:   -g hf \
L00185:   -f prompts/prompt.md \
L00186:   -m defog/llama-3-sqlcoder-8b \
L00187:   -c 0
L00188: ```
L00189: 
L00190: We also support loading a peft adapter here as well via the `-a` flag. Note that the loading of the adapter with the model will take slightly longer than usual.
L00191: 
L00192: ### vLLM
L00193: 
L00194: We also have a [vllm](https://blog.vllm.ai/) runner which uses the vLLM engine to run the inference altogether as a single batch. It is much faster to do so especially when `num_beams` > 1. You would have to pass in a single set of merged model weights, path to LoRA adapters if applicable, and the model architecture needs to be supported by vLLM. Here's a sample command:
L00195: 
L00196: ```bash
L00197: python -W ignore main.py \
L00198:   -db postgres \
L00199:   -q "data/questions_gen_postgres.csv" "data/instruct_basic_postgres.csv" "data/instruct_advanced_postgres.csv" \
L00200:   -o results/vllm_classic.csv results/vllm_basic.csv results/vllm_advanced.csv \
L00201:   -g vllm \
L00202:   -f "prompts/prompt.md" \
L00203:   -m defog/llama-3-sqlcoder-8b \
L00204:   -a path/to_adapter \
L00205:   -c 0
L00206: ```
L00207: 
L00208: Optionally, if you're running evals on a model that is quantized with AWQ, add the `-qz` or `--quantized` parameter. Only applicable for the vllm runner.
L00209: 
L00210: ### Running with an API Server
L00211: 
L00212: If running with different settings, you can setup an api server to avoid reloading for each test setting and then run the tests subsequently. We enable setting up 2 types of api servers, namely the vllm api server, as well as the TGI server.
L00213: 
L00214: We also provide our custom modification of the vllm api server, which only returns the generated output.
L00215: 
L00216: #### VLLM API Server
L00217: 
L00218: ```bash
L00219: # to set up a vllm server
L00220: python -m vllm.entrypoints.api_server \
L00221:     --model defog/defog-llama-3-sqlcoder-8b \
L00222:     --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
L00223:     --dtype float16
L00224: 
L00225: # to set up a vllm server that supports LoRA adapters
L00226: python -m vllm.entrypoints.api_server \
L00227:     --model defog/llama-3-sqlcoder-8b \
L00228:     --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
L00229:     --dtype float16 \
L00230:     --max-model-len 4096 \
L00231:     --enable-lora \
L00232:     --max-lora-rank 64
L00233: 
L00234: # to use our modified api server
L00235: python utils/api_server.py \
L00236:     --model defog/llama-3-sqlcoder-8b \
L00237:     --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
L00238:     --dtype float16 \
L00239:     --max-model-len 4096 \
L00240:     --enable-lora \
L00241:     --max-lora-rank 64
L00242: 
L00243: # to use vllm's openai-compatible api server
L00244: export MODEL_NAME="Qwen/Qwen3-4B"
L00245: vllm serve "$MODEL_NAME" --port 8000
L00246: 
L00247: # to run sql-eval using the api runner - depending on how much your GPUs can take, can increase p and b to higher values
L00248: python main.py \
L00249:   -db postgres \
L00250:   -q "data/questions_gen_postgres.csv" \
L00251:   -o results/api.csv \
L00252:   -g api \
L00253:   -b 1 \
L00254:   -f prompts/prompt.md \
L00255:   --api_url "http://localhost:8000/generate" \
L00256:   --api_type "vllm" \
L00257:   -a path/to_adapter_if_applicable \
L00258:   -p 8
L00259: ```
L00260: 
L00261: #### TGI API Server
L00262: 
L00263: You may consult the [TGI documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/text-generation-inference/quicktour) for more information on how to set up a TGI server. Here's a sample command to set up a TGI server using a preset docker image and run the evaluation using the API runner. Note that you would want to change the number of shards and the model id accordingly, depending on how many gpu's you have available and your model of choice.
L00264: 
L00265: ```bash
L00266: # to set up a tgi server
L00267: model="defog/llama-3-sqlcoder-8b"
L00268: docker run --gpus all \
L00269:   --shm-size 1g \
L00270:   -p 8000:80 \
L00271:   -v /models:/models ghcr.io/huggingface/text-generation-inference:2.0 \
L00272:   --model-id "${model}" \
L00273:   --max-best-of 4 \
L00274:   --max-input-tokens 3072 \
L00275:   --sharded true \
L00276:   --num-shard 4 \
L00277:   --hostname 0.0.0.0 \
L00278:   --port 80
L00279: 
L00280: # to run sql-eval using the api runner - depending on how much your GPUs can take, can increase p and b to higher values. Note that cuda graphs in tgi is optimized for batch sizes that are powers of 2 by default.
L00281: python main.py \
L00282:   -db postgres \
L00283:   -q "data/questions_gen_postgres.csv" \
L00284:   -o results/api.csv \
L00285:   -g api \
L00286:   -b 1 \
L00287:   -f prompts/prompt.md \
L00288:   --api_url "http://localhost:8000/generate" \
L00289:   --api_type "vllm" \
L00290:   -p 8
L00291: ```
L00292: 
L00293: #### Multiple Prompts
L00294: 
L00295: If you'd like to test out a few prompts in a single run (to save the few minutes spent loading the model into GPU at the start of each run), you can specify a list of prompt files in `--prompt_file` (e.g. `-f prompts/prompt-1.md prompts/prompt-2.md prompts/prompt-3.md`), as well as a corresponding list of output files in `--output_file` (e.g. `-o results/results-1.csv results/results-2.csv results/results-3.csv`). The number of prompts and output files must be the same. Here's a sample command:
L00296: 
L00297: ```bash
L00298: python -W ignore main.py \
L00299:   -db postgres \
L00300:   -q "data/questions_gen_postgres.csv" \
L00301:   -o results/results_1.csv results/results_2.csv \
L00302:   -g vllm \
L00303:   -f prompts/prompt_1.md prompts/prompt_2.md \
L00304:   -m defog/sqlcoder2
L00305: ```
L00306: 
L00307: While you can do the same for the other runners, the time savings are most significant when loading a large model locally, vs calling an always-on API.
L00308: 
L00309: #### Thinking Models
L00310: 
L00311: If you'd like to use a model that outputs thinking tokens, you can pass in the flag `--enable_thinking` to the runner so that we will remove the thinking tokens from the LLM output before running the generated query.
L00312: 
L00313: You can check out `run_qwen.sh` for an example of how to run a thinking model.
L00314: 
L00315: ```bash
L00316: ./run_qwen.sh --thinking # add --thinking to generate thinking tokens
L00317: ```
L00318: 
L00319: ### Bedrock
L00320: 
L00321: ```bash
L00322: python -W ignore main.py \
L00323:   -db postgres \
L00324:   -q "data/questions_gen_postgres.csv" \
L00325:   -o results/llama3_70b.csv \
L00326:   -g bedrock \
L00327:   -f prom

L00001: # this file contains all of the helper functions used for evaluations
L00002: 
L00003: import itertools
L00004: import re
L00005: from func_timeout import func_timeout
L00006: import pandas as pd
L00007: from pandas.testing import assert_frame_equal, assert_series_equal
L00008: from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text
L00009: from utils.creds import db_creds_all
L00010: import time
L00011: import collections
L00012: 
L00013: LIKE_PATTERN = r"LIKE[\s\S]*'"
L00014: 
L00015: 
L00016: def deduplicate_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
L00017:     cols = df.columns.tolist()
L00018:     if len(cols) != len(set(cols)):
L00019:         duplicates = [
L00020:             item for item, count in collections.Counter(cols).items() if count > 1
L00021:         ]
L00022:         for dup in duplicates:
L00023:             indices = [i for i, x in enumerate(cols) if x == dup]
L00024:             for i in indices:
L00025:                 cols[i] = f"{dup}_{i}"
L00026:         df.columns = cols
L00027:     return df
L00028: 
L00029: 
L00030: def normalize_table(
L00031:     df: pd.DataFrame, query_category: str, question: str, sql: str = None
L00032: ) -> pd.DataFrame:
L00033:     """
L00034:     Normalizes a dataframe by:
L00035:     1. removing all duplicate rows
L00036:     2. sorting columns in alphabetical order
L00037:     3. sorting rows using values from first column to last (if query_category is not 'order_by' and question does not ask for ordering)
L00038:     4. resetting index
L00039:     """
L00040:     # remove duplicate rows, if any
L00041:     df = df.drop_duplicates()
L00042: 
L00043:     # sort columns in alphabetical order of column names
L00044:     sorted_df = df.reindex(sorted(df.columns), axis=1)
L00045: 
L00046:     # check if query_category is 'order_by' and if question asks for ordering
L00047:     has_order_by = False
L00048:     pattern = re.compile(r"\b(order|sort|arrange)\b", re.IGNORECASE)
L00049:     in_question = re.search(pattern, question.lower())  # true if contains
L00050:     if query_category == "order_by" or in_question:
L00051:         has_order_by = True
L00052: 
L00053:         if sql:
L00054:             # determine which columns are in the ORDER BY clause of the sql generated, using regex
L00055:             pattern = re.compile(r"ORDER BY[\s\S]*", re.IGNORECASE)
L00056:             order_by_clause = re.search(pattern, sql)
L00057:             if order_by_clause:
L00058:                 order_by_clause = order_by_clause.group(0)
L00059:                 # get all columns in the ORDER BY clause, by looking at the text between ORDER BY and the next semicolon, comma, or parantheses
L00060:                 pattern = re.compile(r"(?<=ORDER BY)(.*?)(?=;|,|\)|$)", re.IGNORECASE)
L00061:                 order_by_columns = re.findall(pattern, order_by_clause)
L00062:                 order_by_columns = (
L00063:                     order_by_columns[0].split() if order_by_columns else []
L00064:                 )
L00065:                 order_by_columns = [
L00066:                     col.strip().rsplit(".", 1)[-1] for col in order_by_columns
L00067:                 ]
L00068: 
L00069:                 ascending = False
L00070:                 # if there is a DESC or ASC in the ORDER BY clause, set the ascending to that
L00071:                 if "DESC" in [i.upper() for i in order_by_columns]:
L00072:                     ascending = False
L00073:                 elif "ASC" in [i.upper() for i in order_by_columns]:
L00074:                     ascending = True
L00075: 
L00076:                 # remove whitespace, commas, and parantheses
L00077:                 order_by_columns = [col.strip() for col in order_by_columns]
L00078:                 order_by_columns = [
L00079:                     col.replace(",", "").replace("(", "") for col in order_by_columns
L00080:                 ]
L00081:                 order_by_columns = [
L00082:                     i
L00083:                     for i in order_by_columns
L00084:                     if i.lower()
L00085:                     not in ["desc", "asc", "nulls", "last", "first", "limit"]
L00086:                 ]
L00087: 
L00088:                 # get all columns in sorted_df that are not in order_by_columns
L00089:                 other_columns = [
L00090:                     i for i in sorted_df.columns.tolist() if i not in order_by_columns
L00091:                 ]
L00092: 
L00093:                 # only choose order_by_columns that are in sorted_df
L00094:                 order_by_columns = [
L00095:                     i for i in order_by_columns if i in sorted_df.columns.tolist()
L00096:                 ]
L00097:                 sorted_df = sorted_df.sort_values(
L00098:                     by=order_by_columns + other_columns, ascending=ascending
L00099:                 )
L00100: 
L00101:                 sorted_df = sorted_df[other_columns + order_by_columns]
L00102: 
L00103:     if not has_order_by:
L00104:         # sort rows using values from first column to last
L00105:         sorted_df = sorted_df.sort_values(by=list(sorted_df.columns))
L00106: 
L00107:     # reset index
L00108:     sorted_df = deduplicate_columns(sorted_df)

L00123: # find start and end index of { } in a string. return (start, end) if found, else return (-1, -1)
L00124: def find_bracket_indices(s: str, start_index: int = 0) -> "tuple[int, int]":
L00125:     start = s.find("{", start_index)
L00126:     end = s.find("}", start + 1)

L00132: # extrapolate all possible queries from a query with { } in it
L00133: def get_all_minimal_queries(query: str) -> "list[str]":
L00134:     """
L00135:     extrapolate all possible queries
L00136:     - split by semicolon. this is to accommodate queries where joins to other tables are also acceptable.
L00137:     - expand all column permutations if there are braces { } in it. eg:
L00138:     ```sql
L00139:         SELECT {user.id, user.name} FROM user;
L00140:     ```
L00141:     Would be expanded to:
L00142:     ```sql
L00143:         SELECT user.id FROM user;
L00144:         SELECT user.name FROM user;
L00145:         SELECT user.id, user.name FROM user;
L00146:     ```
L00147:     """
L00148:     queries = query.split(";")
L00149:     result_queries = []
L00150:     for query in queries:
L00151:         query = query.strip()
L00152:         if query == "":
L00153:             continue
L00154:         start, end = find_bracket_indices(query, 0)
L00155:         if (start, end) == (-1, -1):
L00156:             result_queries.append(query)
L00157:             continue
L00158:         else:
L00159:             # get all possible column subsets
L00160:             column_options = query[start + 1 : end].split(",")
L00161:             column_combinations = list(
L00162:                 itertools.chain.from_iterable(
L00163:                     itertools.combinations(column_options, r)
L00164:                     for r in range(1, len(column_options) + 1)
L00165:                 )
L00166:             )
L00167:             for column_tuple in column_combinations:
L00168:                 left = query[:start]
L00169:                 column_str = ", ".join(column_tuple)
L00170:                 right = query[end + 1 :]
L00171:                 # change group by size dynamically if necessary
L00172:                 right = right.replace("GROUP BY {}", f"GROUP BY {column_str}")
L00173:                 result_queries.append(left + column_str + right)
L00174:     return result_queries

L00255:     """

L00257:     After the query is run, the temporary db is dropped.

L00299:                 results_df = results_df.round(decimal_points)
L00300:             conn.close()
L00301:         engine.dispose()  # close connection
L00302: 
L00303:         # remove the temporary database
L00304:         with admin_engine.connect() as conn:
L00305:             conn.execution_options(isolation_level="AUTOCOMMIT")
L00306:             conn.execute(text(f"DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS {db_name}"))
L00307:             conn.close()
L00308:         admin_engine.dispose()  # close connection
L00309: 
L00310:         return results_df
L00311:     except Exception as e:
L00312:         if engine:
L00313:             engine.dispose()
L00314:         if admin_engine:
L00315:             admin_engine.dispose()
L00316:         if conn:
L00317:             conn.close()
